# **The Bay Tribune Daily News — Cycle 112**

### **Inside the Pickup Line: Classroom Realities Behind Rockridge’s Top Mark**
*By Angela Reyes, Education Desk*

At a few minutes past three, the after-school room in Rockridge fills one backpack at a time [1]. Program aide **Mei Wong** stands near the door, learning the children by how they walk through the frame [1]. While citywide tables rank Rockridge at the top of the school quality index at 8.63, Wong notes that parents coming through the door are focused on immediate care rather than statistics [2, 3]:

*   **Mei Wong** (Program Aide) shared what families express at pickup: *"Parents mostly ask about homework and whether their kid ate a real snack, but underneath it's about feeling safe and known... What keeps people here is that sense of community—the same faces at pickup, teachers who remember your kid's name, neighbors who look out. It's not flashy, but it's steady"* [2].
*   **Simone Adesanya** (Principal, Rockridge) addressed the slight index shift from 8.7 down to 8.63 as a minor rounding point on paper [3, 4]: *"Honestly, that dip is a blip on a page to most of us. Teacher quality at 9.08 — that's the number my staff feels every single day, in the hallways... The index is a snapshot; the teachers are the whole album"* [4].
*   **Maya Torres-Dillon** (High School Science Teacher) reflected on the neighborhood’s 94.53% graduation rate and 76.03% college-ready rate among its 247 students [4, 5]: *"Honestly, that 76% number — I recognize it in the hallways more than in any single test score... But I also teach long enough to know that number doesn't capture the kid who's brilliant but has to work nights... What I recognize is the effort behind it"* [5].

While Rockridge gained one student this cycle, enrollment records across Oakland show broader movement at the edges, with West Oakland gaining three students and East Oakland gaining two [6].

### **The Public Safety Record: Incident Counts and Clearance Rates**
*By Sgt. Rachel Torres, Public Safety Desk*

Public safety data across Oakland’s 22 tracked neighborhoods recorded **129 total incidents** this cycle [7]. **Dimond** logged eight incidents—rising three from the prior cycle—tying **Fruitvale** and **West Oakland** for the highest neighborhood total in the city [7]. 

*   **Dimond Metrics:** The neighborhood recorded an average emergency response time of **10.6 minutes** and a **22 percent clearance rate**, supported by a property index of 38 and a violent index of 26 [7].
*   **Citywide Comparisons:** **San Antonio** and **Chinatown** each logged seven incidents [7]. **Temescal** recorded five incidents while logging the slowest average response time in the city at **11.1 minutes** and a **19 percent clearance rate** [7].
*   **Custody Totals:** Across Oakland, 27 arrests occurred during the cycle, leaving **57 individuals in custody** at cycle close and 34 released [8]. In Dimond, eight charges yielded two arrests and three residents held in custody [8].

*By Noah Tan, Metro Desk*

Following a week of overcast skies and fog, Oakland experienced its second consecutive cycle of clear, 48°F weather [9]. Across town, citizens adjusted to the crisp winter air in distinct ways:

*   **Jonas Patel** managed a seasonal health concern during the weather shift [9].

### **Oaks Claim First Franchise Victory; A's Navigate Offseason Math**
*By Selena Grant & Nia Rook, Sports Desk*

*   **Oakland Oaks Inaugural Win:** The expansion **Oakland Oaks** secured the first victory in franchise history, defeating the San Antonio Spurs **97–84** at home to open the regular season 1–0 [11-13]. Rookie **AJ Dybantsa** led all scorers with **25 points and 4 rebounds** [12, 13]. Point guard **Adash Stanley** orchestrated the offense with **17 points and 9 assists**, **Austin Reaves** contributed **14 points, 8 rebounds, and 8 assists**, and **Wendell Carter Jr.** posted a **15-point, 12-rebound double-double** [13, 14]. Head Coach **Wilson Shepard** celebrated his first career win on the bench, noting that his ears were still ringing from the locker room celebration after an 0–9 run through camp and preseason [13, 15].
*   **Oaks Front Office Updates:** Oaks executive **Elias Varek** met with media following the win, confirming that **Atlas Bay Architects** purchased naming rights for **Atlas Bay Stadium** [13, 16]. Varek also disclosed that guard **Jermai Grant** failed his post-trade medical examination and noted that **Draymond Green** remains sidelined with a sprained ankle [13].
*   **Eric Taveras Tops *UNDOCKED*:** World Series champion second baseman **Eric Taveras** leads the *UNDOCKED* game-show leaderboard with **1,170 credits** across two cycles [17, 18]. Taveras confirmed via Moltbook that any prize money will be donated directly to the **Vinnie Keane Firehouse 29 Baseball Academy** in West Oakland [18]. Former third baseman **Martin Richards** (now with the Mets) noted that Taveras benefited from repurposed, clearer game instructions compared to his own zero-credit attempt in Cycle 108 [18].
*   **A's First-Base Succession:** General Manager **Mike Paulson** faces a major offseason choice at the corners [19]. Veteran first baseman **Mark Aitken** (33) enters free agency following a 33-home-run, 87-RBI season (.283 AVG) [19]. Promoting 21-year-old third-base prospect **Kevin Clark** (.297 AVG in 64 ABs) would move **Ernesto Quintero** to first base, presenting a choice between proven veteran production and youth potential [19].
*   **Blue Lantern Farewell:** The **Blue Lantern Bar** in Jack London hosted a community sendoff honoring retiring icons **Vinnie Keane** and **Benji Dillon** [11, 20]. The event brought together fans alongside **Mike Paulson**, **Vladimir Gonzalez**, and **Isley Kelley** [20].

The Top Mark, From the Pickup Line At a few minutes past three, the after-school room in Rockridge starts to fill one backpack at a time. Mei Wong, the program aide, stands near the door and watches who comes in and who gets collected. She has a habit of learning the kids by how they walk through the frame.

Asked what parents want from her, she doesn't reach for the table at all. "Parents mostly ask about homework and whether their kid ate a real snack, but underneath it's about feeling safe and known. They want to know their child is with adults who see them, not just supervising. What keeps people here is that sense of community—the same faces at pickup, teachers who remember your kid's name, neighbors who look out. It's not flashy, but it's steady. That's why families stay even when other places might be growing faster."

The steadiness she describes is what the numbers are trying to measure. Rockridge holds the top school quality index on the table this cycle, at 8.63, ahead of Baylight District and Piedmont Ave among the 22 neighborhoods ranked. Last cycle the same index read 8.7. The dip is small enough that it reads as a rounding question on a page. Inside the building, it is harder to find. Down the hall, Simone Adesanya, the school principal, has her own version of that point. She is not interested in defending a score, and she says so plainly.

"Honestly, that dip is a blip on a page to most of us. Teacher quality at 9.08 — that's the number my staff feels every single day, in the hallways, in the way a kid who was struggling suddenly gets it. The index is a snapshot; the teachers are the whole album. We don't walk around quoting our own score. We walk around making sure every kid in this building knows someone's got their back. That's the real index, and it doesn't move a tenth of a point because of a cycle." The table gives Rockridge a graduation rate of 94.53% and a college-ready rate of 76.03%, with 247 students and funding of 15,000 on the books. Enrollment moved by one student this cycle, from the count last cycle. That is the whole change in the number that moves. Everything else on the table held.

Maya Torres-Dillon teaches high school science here, and she has been on the other side of that 76% for long enough to distrust it a little. She talks about it the way teachers talk about a report card they know is true and also incomplete. "Honestly, that 76% number — I recognize it in the hallways more than in any single test score. It's the kid who stays after class to ask one more question about the lab, or the group that argues about the data until the bell rings. I see it in the parents who show up to every back-to-school night, and in the way my colleagues share lesson plans without being asked. But I also teach long enough to know that number doesn't capture the kid who's brilliant but has to work nights, or the one who freezes on test day. It's a real signal, but it's not the whole story. What I recognize is the effort behind it — and that's something you can't put in a percentage."

As there will undoubtably be moves and decisions by Paulson we will not be able to forsee, there are some we can at least speculate on. The biggest decision being the future of franchise icon Mark Aitken. Aitken who is 33 years old would figure to be on the wron side of his peak years but in 2041 posted some of his best offensive numbers of his career. However similar to Martin Richards being traded away to allow the everyday bats for Ernesto Quintero the same script may be the one to read for Kevin Clark. Clark who flashed some potential this past season figures to get everyday at bats which would naturally move Quintero to his second position, first base. Its possible that the emergence of Ernesto Quintero will ultimately seal the fate of Richards and Aitken. Carmen Mesa had looked to be the front runner to take Benji Dillon place in the rotation next season until Pablo Almanzar cemented himself in that slot. Does Mesa return to AAA or will Mesa be moved? Desmond Morton and Frank Reyna are completing for the 1 everyday spot in the OF that is available. The other would be the forth outfielder. This is a story to watch that shapes itself alot like last years decision between Vladimir Gonzales and Peter Busch. Both players figure to have a great career, but you cant keep everyone. Lastly, the bullpen showed some cracks late in the season and the mix of veterans and young arms may need a refresh. As many of the bullpen spots are likely accounted for is their a high end free agent signing that can makes sense.
